title: 2022_PMC9707357_Sociodemographic_Variation_in_Early_Uptake_of_COVID-19_Vaccine_a
ehr_evidence: CDC analyzed data from 4,496 National Immunization Survey-Child COVID Module (NIS-CCM) interviews conducted during July 1–29, 2022; NIS-CCM is an ongoing, national random-digit–dialed mobile telephone survey of households that include children and adolescents aged 6 months–17 years.
summary: A cross-sectional national random-digit-dialed telephone survey of 4,496 parents of children aged 6 months–4 years examining sociodemographic variation in early COVID-19 vaccine uptake and parental intent and attitudes in the United States.
key_findings: 3.5% of children aged 6 months–4 years had received ≥1 dose of COVID-19 vaccine; 59.3% were unvaccinated but parent open to vaccination, and 37.2% were unvaccinated and parent reluctant to vaccinate.

Openness to vaccination was higher among parents of Asian (83.1%), Hispanic (66.2%), and Black (61.1%) children than White (52.9%) children, and lower among parents of children in rural areas (45.8%) than urban areas (64.1%).
Higher vaccination coverage was observed among children in households with income >$75,000/yr and higher maternal educational attainment versus lower-income and lower-education households.
Parental confidence in COVID-19 vaccine safety and receipt of a provider recommendation were lower among unvaccinated than vaccinated children.
Approximately three fourths (78.5%) of vaccinated children received their vaccine at a medical setting.
captured_features: parental intent to vaccinate (open vs reluctant)
parental attitudes (concern, importance, safety perception, provider recommendation, difficulty)
population: Parents/guardians of children aged 6 months–4 years in the United States (n=4,496)
exposure_domain: Sociodemographic characteristics (race/ethnicity, household income, maternal education, urban-rural residence, social vulnerability index) and parental attitudes/beliefs about COVID-19 vaccine
limitations: Vaccination status and intent were parent-reported and subject to recall and social desirability biases.
